summary: Jesus goes home to Nazareth and is dismissed by people who watched him grow up — Mark says he could do almost nothing there. He sends the Twelve out in pairs with instructions to carry nothing, and while they are gone Mark stops the narrative to tell how Herod Antipas had John the Baptist beheaded at a birthday party. The disciples return exhausted, a crowd of five thousand follows them to a deserted place, and Jesus feeds all of them from five loaves. That night he walks across the lake to their struggling boat.
whyItMatters: This is the chapter where the cost gets named. John, the man who opened the book, is killed for telling a ruler the truth — and Mark places that execution in the middle of the disciples' first mission trip, so the reader learns what the job is before the disciples do.

context.author: Anonymous; early tradition names Mark, recording Peter's preaching
context.audience: Greek-speaking readers outside Judea; Mark uses the Roman 'fourth watch of the night' rather than a Jewish time reckoning
context.setting: Nazareth, the villages of Galilee, Herod's court, and a deserted place by the lake
context.literaryForm: Narrative with another Mark sandwich — the mission of the Twelve is split open and John's death is set inside it

outline.heading: Rejected at home
outline.note: They know his family and his trade, and that settles it for them

outline.heading: The Twelve sent out — outer half
outline.note: Two by two, no bread, no bag, no money

outline.heading: John beheaded — inner half
outline.note: A flashback triggered by Herod's guilty guess about who Jesus is

outline.heading: They come back
outline.note: Too tired to eat; the rest is interrupted by a crowd that runs ahead on foot

outline.heading: Five thousand fed
outline.note: 'You give them something to eat' — five loaves, two fish, twelve baskets left

outline.heading: Walking on the water
outline.note: He intends to pass by; they think he is a ghost; Mark blames their hardened hearts

keyVerses.text: Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James, Joses, Judah, and Simon? Aren’t his sisters here with us?
keyVerses.why: The most ordinary description of Jesus anywhere in the gospels, spoken as a reason to dismiss him.

keyVerses.text: he had compassion on them because they were like sheep without a shepherd
keyVerses.why: Mark tells you the motive before the miracle. The feeding starts as pity, not as a demonstration.

keyVerses.text: You give them something to eat.
keyVerses.why: He hands the problem back to the men who wanted it sent away.

keyVerses.text: for they hadn’t understood about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.
keyVerses.why: One of the harshest lines Mark writes about the disciples — and it comes immediately after a miracle they took part in.

questions.question: Verse 5 says he 'could do no mighty work there.' Does that mean unbelief limits him?
questions.answer: It is a striking sentence and Matthew softens it when he retells this ('did not do many mighty works'), which suggests it read as strong even then. Mark's own qualifier is in the same verse: he did lay hands on a few sick people and heal them, so it is not absolute. The most natural reading is relational rather than mechanical — these healings happen where someone comes and asks, and in Nazareth almost nobody did. He does not overrule a town that has decided it already knows him.

questions.question: Why is being called 'the carpenter, the son of Mary' an insult?
questions.answer: Two things are doing work. First, a manual trade placed him socially — this is the only place in the gospels where Jesus himself is given the trade, and the point is that they know exactly what he is and it isn't a teacher. Second, men were normally identified by their father, so 'son of Mary' is unusual. Readers differ on whether it hints at a slur about his birth or simply means Joseph had died. Either way the sentence is doing the work of a shrug: we know this family, so there is nothing here.

questions.question: Jesus had brothers and sisters?
questions.answer: Mark names four brothers and refers to sisters. How to understand that has divided Christians for a long time. Most Protestants read it plainly as later children of Mary and Joseph. Catholic tradition holds that the Greek word for brother can cover close kin such as cousins, and that Mary remained a virgin. Orthodox tradition generally takes them as Joseph's children from an earlier marriage. Mark himself gives no ruling; he is quoting neighbours, not writing a family record.

questions.question: Why send them out with nothing?
questions.answer: The packing list is severe — a staff and sandals, no bread, no bag, no money, one tunic. Practically it forces dependence on hospitality, which was a strong social obligation in that culture, and it means every town has to decide whether to receive them. It also strips out anything that would make them look like travelling philosophers making a living from lectures. They arrive with nothing to sell.

questions.question: What does shaking the dust off your feet mean?
questions.answer: A recognized gesture of separation. Travellers returning from Gentile territory were said to shake off its dust before re-entering the land, so doing it as you leave a Jewish town is pointed: you have placed yourselves outside. It is a public statement that the matter has been put to them and they declined, and that the responsibility now rests with them. Note it is a departure, not a threat carried out — they leave rather than argue.

questions.question: Why does Mark stop the story to tell how John died?
questions.answer: The trigger is Herod's guilty conscience in verse 16 — he hears about Jesus and assumes John has come back. But the placement is deliberate. The Twelve go out preaching repentance; Mark cuts to what happened to the last man who preached repentance to someone powerful; then the Twelve come back full of what they accomplished. The reader now knows something they do not. This is the same interruption technique Mark uses in chapters 3, 5, 11 and 14.

questions.question: Herod didn't even want to kill John. Why did he?
questions.answer: Mark says he feared John, considered him righteous and holy, protected him, and liked listening to him — and then killed him anyway. The stated reason is his oath and his dinner guests. He had made a public promise in front of the important men of Galilee and would not lose face by breaking it. It is one of the bleakest pieces of character writing in the gospels: a man does something he knows is wrong, and profoundly regrets, because backing down in front of the room felt worse.

questions.question: Which Herod is this? There seem to be several.
questions.answer: There are, and they are easy to confuse. Herod the Great, who ruled at Jesus's birth, died around 4 BC. This is his son Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea for Rome — the one who executed John and who appears again at Jesus's trial in Luke. A different son, Philip, is named here as Herodias's first husband. The family kept recycling the name, which is why the gospels usually add a detail to say which one they mean.

questions.question: What is a denarius, and how much bread is two hundred of them?
questions.answer: A denarius was roughly a day's wage for an ordinary labourer. Two hundred denarii is therefore something like eight months of work — the disciples are naming an absurd figure to make the point that the request is impossible. That is the setup for what follows: five loaves and two fish, which is somebody's lunch.

questions.question: Why does it say twelve baskets left over? Is the number meaningful?
questions.answer: Almost certainly. Twelve is the number of the tribes of Israel and of the men he had just sent out — and this feeding happens on the Jewish side of the lake. In chapter 8 he feeds four thousand on the Gentile side and there are seven baskets left. Mark makes the disciples recite both numbers back to him in 8:19-20, which is a strong signal that he wants the reader counting.

questions.question: Verse 48 says 'he would have passed by them.' Why would he walk past his own struggling disciples?
questions.answer: It reads oddly in English, and it is probably an intentional echo. In the Hebrew scriptures, God 'passes by' Moses and Elijah as the way of revealing himself (Exodus 33:19-22, 1 Kings 19:11). On that reading, passing by is not indifference but a form of showing — and the phrase 'It is I' in verse 50 is the same construction used for the divine name in Exodus 3:14. Mark reports it without explanation and lets readers who know those passages hear the echo.

questions.question: Why does Mark say their hearts were hardened right after they saw the loaves multiplied?
questions.answer: Because that is his point about miracles. They had handled the bread themselves and gathered the leftovers, and it did not translate into recognizing who was in the boat with them. Mark uses 'hardened' for the opposition in 3:5 — using the same word for the Twelve is deliberate and unflattering. Seeing something extraordinary is not the same as understanding it, which is one of the book's steadiest claims.

glossary.def: The Greek word covers a builder working in wood and stone — a general craftsman rather than specifically a furniture maker.
Son of Herod the Great; Rome's client ruler over Galilee and Perea. Not a king in Roman law, though Mark uses the popular title.
A Roman silver coin, about a day's pay for a labourer. The measure the disciples reach for when estimating the impossible.
Roughly 3 to 6 a.m. Mark divides the night into four Roman watches rather than the three used in Jewish reckoning — a small sign of who he was writing for.
A phrase from the Hebrew scriptures (Numbers 27:17, Ezekiel 34) describing a people whose leaders have failed them. Mark places it immediately after Herod's banquet, which sharpens it.
